teach.title: By how much
teach.say: When you want to say not just 'taller' but 'much taller', the measure of the gap goes into the ablative: **the ablative of degree (the 'by how much' form: multō māior = bigger by much)**. *Mārcus multō altior est quam Quīntus* — Marcus is taller than Quintus by much. The measuring word stands beside the comparative (the '-er / more' form) and answers one question only: by how much?

check.ask: Which word here says how big the difference is?

teach.title: multō: by much
teach.say: *multō* is the everyday one. It is the ablative of *multum*, and it means 'by much'. It sits immediately in front of the comparative it measures: *multō altior* much taller, *multō gravior* much heavier, *multō melior* much better. English puts *much* in exactly the same place.

check.ask: Mare hodiē ____ altius est. Which word makes 'deeper' into 'much deeper'?

teach.title: paulō: by a little
teach.say: *paulō* is its opposite number, 'by a little': *paulō brevior* a little shorter, *paulō frīgidior* a little colder. Both words end in *-ō* because that is the ablative singular of an *-us -a -um* adjective standing on its own, with no noun: literally 'by much', 'by a little'.

check.ask: Aqua in impluviō ____ frīgidior est. Which word means 'by a little'?

teach.title: paulō ante, paulō post
teach.say: The same measure works with words that already point earlier or later: *paulō ante* a little before, *paulō post* a little afterwards. Nothing is compared with *quam* here, and nothing needs to be: what *paulō* measures is the gap between that moment and this one — how much earlier, how much later.

check.ask: Which word here measures how much earlier the ship sails?

teach.title: Two ablatives, two jobs
teach.say: Not every ablative near a comparative is a measure. In *mīles gladiō pugnat*, *gladiō* is **the ablative (the 'by/with/from' form)** — the tool he fights with. In *multō longiōre gladiō*, *gladiō* is still the tool and *multō* answers 'by how much?'. Ask the question aloud: 'with what?' gives the means, 'by how much?' gives the degree. A plain 'than' is a third thing again, and comes with *quam*: *multō fortior quam ille*.

check.ask: Which word here measures the gap between the two soldiers?

core.text: When you say *bigger by a lot* or *higher by ten feet*, the measure goes in the ablative: **the ablative of degree (the 'by how much' form: multo maior = bigger by much)**. *multō* (by much) and *paulō* (by a little) are the everyday ones: *terra multō pulchrior* — a land more beautiful by much, much more beautiful; *nāvis paulō levior fit* — the ship becomes a little lighter. The ablative sits next to a comparative (the '-er / more' form) and says how far apart the two things are. Latin name: ablātīvus mēnsūrae.
English says *much bigger*, *ten feet higher*: the word before the *-er* form measures the gap. Latin puts that word in the ablative, which here means *by*.
multō / paulō / a measured amount, in the ablative, beside a comparative = 'by so much'.

invented.la: Frāter meus multō altior est quam ego.
invented.en: My brother is much taller than I am.

core.text: Two ablatives can stand near one comparative. *multō* answers *by how much?*; the ablative of comparison (the 'than' form: illo fortior = braver than he) answers *than whom?*. *Hic multō fortior est illō* — braver than that one (*illō*) by much (*multō*). A measure is degree; the thing compared is comparison.

more.text: Any measurement works: *decem pedibus altior* — ten feet higher. The same ablative goes with words that hide a comparison, above all time words: *paulō post* — a little later; *multō ante* — long before; *paulō ante* — a little earlier (*quantī paulō ante* — as big as a little before). It also goes with *magis* (more) and *minus* (less): *multō magis laetābor* — I shall be much happier.
*tantō … quantō* — by so much … by how much: *quantō altior mōns, tantō frīgidior āēr* — the higher the mountain, the colder the air. *nihilō* (by nothing) makes *nihilō minus* — none the less.

The learner's notes (week 16): the ablative names the degree of difference between two things compared; it is either a unit of measure (*pēs* foot, *ūncia* inch, *passus* pace) or a general quantity word (*multum, paulum*); it can combine with a *quam* clause or with an ablative of comparison: *hic multō fortior est*, *hic multō fortior est illō*, *hī paulō māiōrēs sunt quam illī*, *mūrus decem pedibus altior est*. Ørberg (chapter XVI): *multō pulchriōrem, multō turbidior, multō altiōrēs, paulō levior*; A&G §414 call it the ablative of degree of difference.
